Documentation & Reporting

Nursing records, reporting, legal rules and methods such as SOAP and narrative.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • State the purposes of nursing records
  • Describe methods of documentation
  • List legal rules for recording and reporting

In simple words

Documentation is writing down what the nurse assessed, did and the patient’s response. It is a legal record and a way to communicate with the whole health team.

Good documentation is accurate, complete, current and organised. If it is not written, it is not done.

Purposes of records

  • Communicate with the health team.
  • Show the care given and the patient’s response.
  • Serve as a legal document.
  • Help with audit, research and billing.
  • Plan continuity of care.

Methods of documentation

Method What it is
Narrative Writing the story of care in paragraphs
SOAP Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan
Problem-oriented Listing problems, goals and progress
Charting by exception Writing only abnormal or significant findings

Legal rules

  • Write in ink, in black or blue.
  • Date, time and sign every entry.
  • Do not erase; cross out errors with one line and initial.
  • Write facts, not opinions.
  • Never chart ahead of time or for someone else.
  • Record late entries as “late entry” with the actual time.

🔴 Legal rule

If it is not written, it is not done. Records are legal documents — write facts, date, time and sign every entry.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Nursing notes — write after every procedure, observation or change in condition.
  • Incident reports — record what happened, who was involved, and action taken.
  • Handover — written notes help the next shift continue care safely.
  • Legal cases — your chart may be used as evidence; keep it truthful.
  • Audit — records show whether standards of care were met.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Documentation communicates care to the health team and is a legal record.
  2. Methods: narrative, SOAP, problem-oriented, charting by exception.
  3. SOAP = Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.
  4. Write in ink; date, time and sign every entry.
  5. Do not erase — cross out errors with one line, initial and date.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Write facts, not opinions.
  2. Never chart ahead of time or for someone else.
  3. Record late entries as late entries with the actual time.

📌 Memory trick

Charting rules: “DTS” — Date, Time, Sign. Every entry needs DTS.

60-second revision

  • Records are legal; if not written, not done.
  • Methods: narrative, SOAP, problem-oriented, exception.
  • SOAP = Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.
  • Ink, date, time, sign; facts not opinions.
  • Cross out errors with one line, initial and date.

Test yourself

In SOAP, 'A' stands for:

Answer: A. A is Assessment — the nurse's conclusion about the patient's problem.

Documentation should be done in:

Answer: B. Nursing records are written in ink so they cannot be easily altered.

If you make an error in a record, you should:

Answer: B. Cross out with a single line, then initial and date.

Charting by exception means:

Answer: B. Charting by exception records only abnormal or significant findings, not routine normal ones.

Records should never be:

Answer: C. Never chart ahead of time — record only what you actually did or observed.
